solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Who’s put out about a boxer? (8)

indicators.note: letters that are put out are thrown into disorder
the rearranged letters go round A

blocks.note: anagram fodder, rearranged
placed inside, between P and W

annotation.surface: Someone is asking which boxer has been left upset.
annotation.walkthrough: A southpaw is a left-handed boxer, leading with the right hand and foot. "Who’s put out" reads as a question about hurt feelings.
annotation.definitionFit: Southpaw is the name for a boxer who fights left-handed.

blocks.note: the chemical symbol for oxygen
a zone is a region

annotation.surface: A description of an area filled with oxygen gas.
annotation.walkthrough: "Region of oxygen" is read as oxygen's region: O-ZONE, the O coming first. Ozone is itself a form of oxygen, which makes the surface nearly true.
annotation.definitionFit: Ozone is a gas, a form of oxygen with three atoms to the molecule.

entries.clue: Growing up, miss your old man? (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters read bottom to top
THY is the old form of your

blocks.note: to omit is to miss out; it grows up to TIMO
archaic your

annotation.surface: A child, growing up, asks whether you miss your father.
annotation.walkthrough: "Your old man" wants to mean a father; "old" in fact only turns your into THY, and "man" is left alone as the definition: a man's name.
annotation.definitionFit: The definition is a name by example: 'man' stands for any man's name, and Timothy is one.

blocks.note: owned: the past tense of possess
wild, as if gripped by a demon

annotation.surface: Someone claims that to have something is to be mad.
annotation.walkthrough: Two different senses: owned, and gripped by a frenzy as if by a demon.
annotation.definitionFit: Possessed means had (owned) and, as an adjective, wild or mad.

blocks.note: to whip is slang for to steal
as in ten pounds a head, ten pounds per head
snappers are fish; fish can be plural

annotation.surface: Naughty children pinch a fish.
annotation.walkthrough: "A fish" looks singular, but A is PER and fish stands as a plural, giving SNAPPERS.
annotation.definitionFit: Whippersnappers are impertinent young people.

blocks.note: guff is empty talk
aw, shame: the exclamation of sympathy

annotation.surface: A laugh that is all hot air is a shame.
annotation.walkthrough: "Shame" is the exclamation ("What a shame!"), for which AW is the sound of sympathy.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the noun: a guffaw is the loud, belly kind of laugh.

entries.clue: Energy making one blow one’s top (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a gust is a single blow of wind
the first letter of one

annotation.surface: Enough energy to make someone blow their top.
annotation.walkthrough: "Blow one’s top" reads as losing one's temper; it splits into blow (GUST) and the top of "one".
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of zest: doing something with gusto is doing it with energy.

blocks.note: additional, as in more details
the verb: to help a cause along

annotation.surface: A call for more aid.
annotation.walkthrough: "More aid" reads as one phrase; it is two definitions side by side, the second a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: as an adjective it means additional, and as a verb to advance a cause is to help it.

entries.clue: It’s easy killing one immobile deer (1,4,4)

blocks.note: the indefinite article, one of something
held fast, unable to move
a male deer

annotation.surface: Shooting a deer that cannot move is no challenge.
annotation.walkthrough: The hunting picture hides a money sense: a killing is a big profit, and a fast buck is money made easily.
annotation.definitionFit: A fast buck is money made quickly and easily, an easy killing.

blocks.note: used just as it stands
Royal Marines

annotation.surface: An army with no soldiers, as usual.
annotation.walkthrough: RM, the Royal Marines, is a standard crossword abbreviation for soldiers.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the norm is the usual level against which things are measured.

blocks.note: a slip is a petticoat
burn is the Scottish word for a stream

annotation.surface: Laundry instructions: wash the petticoat, then burn it.
annotation.walkthrough: "Wash" is the noun: the churned air or water left behind a propeller or boat. A burn is a Scottish stream, not a fire.
annotation.definitionFit: A slipstream is the wash of air or water behind a moving craft.

entries.clue: Met person with the other paper round (7,7)

indicators.note: the letters are turned round into a new order

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Meeting a delivery person who carries a rival newspaper on their round.
annotation.walkthrough: "Met" is not the past of meet but the Met Office, Britain's national weather service, so a Met person is a forecaster. "Paper round" is a newspaper delivery route.
annotation.definitionFit: A weather prophet forecasts the weather, the business of the Met Office.

indicators.note: the years come after the other piece

blocks.note: sat out rather than play
abbreviation

annotation.surface: Some lechers, in later years, gave up playing.
annotation.walkthrough: Satyrs were the goat-legged companions of Bacchus in Greek myth, hence the lecherous sense. The commas make "later" look like a comment on time rather than a placement instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Satyrs are lustful men, after the goat-men of Greek myth.

entries.clue: Where Turkey is while I’m visiting Oregon (4,5)

blocks.note: as = while, of two things at once
I'm written out as I AM
visiting a place is being in it
the US state abbreviation

annotation.surface: A traveller in Oregon wonders where Turkey is.
annotation.walkthrough: "Turkey" reads as the Thanksgiving bird, apt for an American state; it is the country, which occupies Asia Minor.
annotation.definitionFit: Asia Minor, or Anatolia, is the peninsula making up most of Turkey.

indicators.note: the word stops one letter short

blocks.note: to cook the books is to rig them
cricket scoring abbreviation
ROUSE (fire up), without its last E

annotation.surface: A recipe: cooking something over a fire until it is nearly tough.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen picture misleads: cook means fiddle, and fire means stir up.
annotation.definitionFit: Rigorous means strict and demanding, tough.

entries.clue: One we get to deploy around start of brawl? (2-7)

annotation.definition: One we get to deploy around start of brawl?

indicators.note: deploying the letters spreads them into a new order
the rearranged letters surround B
only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters
goes inside, after GO

annotation.surface: When a fight is about to break out, a mediator is the person we send in.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the wordplay builds the answer, and read as a sentence it describes the go-between sent in when a brawl starts.
annotation.definitionFit: A go-between is an intermediary deployed between two parties in dispute.

entries.clue: One island, rocky, but not a dangerous place (5,3)

indicators.note: unsteady, so the letters are shaken up
the letter A is taken out

blocks.note: anagram fodder, before the A goes
the A removed, leaving ONEISLND to rearrange

annotation.surface: An island that is rocky but still not dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: A rocky island sounds hazardous; "rocky" is the anagram signal, and the clue then says it is not dangerous while the answer is.
annotation.definitionFit: A lion's den is a place of great danger.

entries.clue: Discover how to subtly get in the way? (4,3)

annotation.definition2: how to subtly get in the way?

blocks.note: to find by sniffing around, like a dog

blocks.clueFragment: how to subtly get in the way?
blocks.note: edging a car's front gently out into traffic, claiming the road

annotation.surface: A driver works out how to edge into traffic without causing trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: To nose out is to sniff out a secret, and also to edge a car's nose out gradually into a road, a subtle way of getting in the traffic's way; the question mark flags that second, playful definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To nose out is to discover by searching, and to ease forward nose first.

blocks.note: bam is an old word for a hoax
used just as it stands
knockout

annotation.surface: A cheeky con with a stunning finish.
annotation.walkthrough: "Capital" poses as an adjective (excellent) before hoax; it is the noun, a capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the city is the seat of government of Mali in West Africa.

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it inside, so ROM goes around DATA
about can mean turned round, as in about-face, so the whole is turned round

blocks.note: a Rom is a Romani person; it holds the next piece
inside ROM: RO-DATA-M, which is then turned round

annotation.surface: A Romani man is hiding the truth about a murderer.
annotation.walkthrough: The killer is a bullfighter, who kills the bull.
annotation.definitionFit: A matador is the bullfighter who delivers the killing stroke.

blocks.note: the answer's first word is itself the anagram signal, saying what was done to the clue's letters
the letters of the clue's first words, rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone taking a poet's side in a dispute.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer describes the clue: TO A POETS, mashed up, gives POTATOES. "Side" is a side dish.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a side is a side dish, and mash is the classic one served with a main course.

indicators.note: the answer is held inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words, after the first three letters of contempt

annotation.surface: Someone despised, yet still at liberty.
annotation.walkthrough: "Free" means vacant, as a seat or room is free.
annotation.definitionFit: Free in the sense of vacant, as a seat or room can be free, with nobody in it.

entries.clue: Course of training upset a few but not all (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, set upside down: the letters read upward
the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: physical education; turned up to EP
SOME without its E

annotation.surface: A training course upsets a few of the trainees, though not everyone.
annotation.walkthrough: "Course" is a racecourse: Epsom Downs in Surrey, home of the Derby.
annotation.definitionFit: Epsom is a racecourse, where the Derby is run.

entries.clue: Wanting, during contest, to cross line (10)

indicators.note: the L crosses into the middle of the contest word

blocks.note: in the course of, as in the night
to compete is to contest; it takes L inside
abbreviation

annotation.surface: Someone longing, mid-competition, to be first over the line.
annotation.walkthrough: "Wanting" means lacking, not desiring.
annotation.definitionFit: Wanting means lacking something, so incomplete.

blocks.note: to dis is to belittle
as on road signs

annotation.surface: Someone disparages hospital food.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hospital food" reads as one familiar complaint; food is the definition alone.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by the wider class: the word names a prepared course, as in dish of the day, which is food.

indicators.note: PREY forms walls around TT

blocks.note: the hunted animal; it surrounds the next piece
teetotal, so not drinking

annotation.surface: A quarry whose walls are fairly dry.
annotation.walkthrough: "Quarry" pictures a stone pit; it is the hunted animal. TT (teetotal) is the usual crossword dry.
annotation.definitionFit: An adverb of degree: in pretty good the word means fairly, so the two swap in a sentence.

indicators.note: we are told how it sounds

blocks.note: sinned = offended, roam = tramp

annotation.surface: A tramp who has been insulted is causing a disturbance.
annotation.walkthrough: "Offended" means transgressed, not upset, and "tramp" is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A syndrome is a medical disorder, a set of symptoms occurring together.
